segments.say: It's Sunday evening, and the light outside the window is going soft and grey. Tomas sits on the sofa with his phone in his hand, scrolling slowly. There are dozens of names in his messages. Dozens of little notes and pictures and quick replies from the past few days. And yet, as the flat grows quiet around him, a small thought rises up and refuses to leave. When did I last actually talk to someone?

show.sub: The phone is full of names

segments.say: Before we go on, a quick word about Tomas. He is imagined. He's someone we've pictured together, to keep company with us through tonight's ideas. He's in his early thirties, he works from home in a small city flat, and he's kind, capable and perfectly ordinary. Nothing here happened to him, and it doesn't need to. We borrow him because his Sunday evening might look a little like one of yours.

His week hasn't been empty. That's the strange part. He answered emails, joined video calls, replied to group chats, and sent a good many cheerful messages. Everything looks perfectly fine from the outside. But the evening has a particular hush to it, and in that hush he notices something that no list of messages can quite hide. He has talked a lot this week. He just hasn't really been heard.

If you know that feeling, even a little, you're welcome here. Nothing is wrong with you for noticing it. In fact, it's one of the oldest and most studied feelings in psychology. And like many familiar feelings, it's wrapped in ideas that sound completely sensible, but that science has quietly looked at again. So let's start gently, with the feeling itself, and with what it actually is.

Psychologists Letitia Anne Peplau and Daniel Perlman, working in the early 1980s, described loneliness in a way that has stayed useful ever since. It's the painful gap between the connection we want and the connection we have. Notice what that doesn't say. It doesn't mention how many people are around you, or how many names are in your phone. It's about the distance between what you hope for and what you actually receive. That gap is the whole feeling.

show.text: Loneliness is the gap between the connection we want and the connection we have.

segments.say: Which means loneliness isn't a character flaw, and it isn't a sign that someone is boring, or broken, or hard to love. It's a feeling that appears when the connection a person has doesn't match the connection they long for. Anyone can have it. Busy people, popular people, people with full calendars and kind friends. Tomas included. It simply says that something he needs, and values, is a little out of reach tonight.

Here is where we're going tonight. We'll ask whether lonely simply means alone. Whether it's just a feeling that means nothing. Whether social pain is real pain. What the lonely brain does with other people. How loneliness touches sleep and the body. Who actually feels it most. Where social media fits in. And what really seems to help. We'll go slowly, and we'll check each idea against what researchers have actually found.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore
items: Whether it's just a feeling that means nothing
Whether social pain is real pain
What the lonely brain does with other people
How loneliness touches sleep and the body

segments.say: It's worth saying early that this is one of the most common human feelings there is. Almost everyone feels it at some point, in some season of life, whether it's after a move, a change of job, a loss, or for no obvious reason at all. If it's visiting you now, you're not an exception. You're simply one of a very large number of people who have felt a gap, and wished it were smaller.

Here's a small thought to keep with you, not from any study. Loneliness is a feeling, not a verdict. A verdict is final. A feeling is something that arrives, says its piece, and can change. Whatever you find out tonight, you can hold it that way. Nobody here is going to tell you what you should have done differently, or who you ought to have become by now.

show.text: Loneliness is a feeling, not a verdict.

segments.say: Now, there's a reason we're going to look at these ideas one by one. Most of us have picked up a handful of beliefs about loneliness, mostly from conversations, films and passing remarks. Some of them are partly true. Some are kinder than the truth, and some are harsher. They tend to be called myths when they're held a bit too firmly, and a good myth is just a half-truth that has never been gently questioned.

When we call something a myth tonight, it won't be a scolding. Nobody is silly for believing it. If you've ever thought that loneliness is just a matter of being alone, or that you ought to be able to shake it off, then you were thinking the way a great many thoughtful people do. We'll simply look at each idea, see what researchers measured, and ask what it might mean for Tomas, and for you.

Let's look around Tomas's flat for a moment. It's small, tidy, and warm. A laptop sits closed on the desk by the window. A plant on the shelf has just begun to lean toward the light. A mug of tea is going cold beside him, and he hasn't noticed.
From this window you can see other windows, other lamps, other evenings, each one lit up and a little out of reach.

show.sub: Lit up and out of reach

segments.say: He looks out at the street, where the lights are coming on one by one. It's a very ordinary sight. Somewhere in each of those windows, someone is cooking, or tidying, or sitting very still. And it's a curious thing that a city can hold so many people so close together, and still, for a moment, make a person feel as though they are watching life through glass.

Tomas's phone lights up with another message in the group chat. It's a joke, and a picture, and three reactions. He smiles a little, and types a reply. And somewhere in the middle of that, he realizes something quite specific. None of it feels like the kind of contact he's hungry for. It's pleasant, and it's friendly, and he's glad it's there. But it doesn't reach the place where the quiet question sits.

This is where the old definition helps. The gap isn't between Tomas and other people. It's between the connection he wants and the connection he has. Many of us wouldn't call a funny picture in a group chat a real conversation, and that's honest. It tells him that what he wants is something warmer and slower. Something where somebody asks how he is, and waits for the answer.

There's something quietly hopeful in that. A feeling that points to something specific is much easier to work with than a vague gloom. If Tomas knows that what he misses is a real exchange, one voice and one listener, then he knows what to look for. And that means tonight isn't a sad evening to get through. It's an evening to understand a little more clearly.

show.text: A feeling that points to something specific is easier to work with.

segments.say: One more thing, before we begin. At no point tonight will anybody be blamed. Not Tomas, and not you. Loneliness is never evidence that a person did something wrong. People get lonely for reasons that have more to do with life, timing and circumstance than with who they are. So you can listen the way you'd listen to a good friend describing a tricky stretch of road.
You might wonder why we'd bother to understand it at all. Why not just distract ourselves, and let the feeling pass? Sometimes that's exactly right.

But often, knowing what's happening makes a feeling lighter to carry. It stops being a mysterious weight, and starts being something with a shape, and a purpose, and some quite surprising science behind it.

So let's begin with the first question, the one Tomas is quietly asking himself on the sofa. He's surrounded by messages, and yet he feels alone. Does that mean he's mixing up two different things? Does being lonely always mean being by yourself? It turns out that researchers have thought hard about this exact question, and their answer is gentler and more interesting than you might expect.

Think of the two words we've been using. Alone, and lonely. In everyday speech we treat them like neighbors, and often like twins. But look at them closely and you notice that one describes where you are, and the other describes how you feel. One can be counted. The other can only be felt. And if they were really the same thing, you'd expect them to move together every single time.

Imagine Tomas at a busy party, surrounded by cheerful people, laughing politely at the right moments, and feeling quite far from every one of them. Now imagine him, on another day, walking alone in a quiet park, entirely at ease with his own company. Same man, same city, two very different inner weather systems. The number of people nearby hasn't decided either one.

show.text: The number of people nearby hasn't decided either one.

segments.say: So here's the first idea we'll look at, an idea you may well have heard said out loud. Lonely just means alone. It sounds like plain common sense. It also happens to be one of the easiest ideas to test, because we can measure how many people someone sees, and we can ask how they feel, and then check whether those two things line up.

show.sub: A first myth to look at

segments.say: Before we look at what the researchers found, take a slow breath in, and let it out. There's no rush tonight. The evening is long, and we have plenty of time for every question. Tomas has made a fresh cup of tea, and he's sitting a little straighter on the sofa. Whatever he and you are about to learn, nobody has to do anything with it right away.
